# How often does MIKAI interrupt you for nothing? A first, honest count

*Draft · 2026-10-13 · not published. Generated by `python3 eval/dismiss_rate.py` against `~/.mikai/notification_log.db`.*

## Why this number

Every proactive AI assistant launched this year measures whether it can *finish a task*. None publishes how often its unprompted messages were worth the interruption. That ratio is the one MIKAI is built around: a message you didn't ask for costs attention, so the assistant should be judged on how rarely it wastes it.

**Dismiss rate** = interruptions you dismissed ÷ interruptions you either dismissed or acted on.

Lower is better. Our target, set before any data came in: **under 30% once at least 20 interruptions have a recorded response.**

## The current number

| | |
|---|---|
| Decisions made (send or stay silent) | 31 |
| Interruptions sent | 23 |
| Stayed silent | 8 (2 by choice, 6 failed to run) |
| Sent items with any recorded response | 3 of 23 (13%) |
| Acted on | 0 |
| Dismissed | 3 (all inferred, none explicit) |
| **Dismiss rate** | **100%, from 3 data points** |
| Target check (under 30% after 20) | **Not evaluable yet** (3 of 20 needed) |

Period covered: 28 June to 7 August 2026, one user (the builder). The engine has been switched off since 7 August.

**Plainly: this number means almost nothing yet.** Three data points can't distinguish a bad assistant from bad measurement, and the measurement here was weak (see below). We're publishing the method and the starting point so later numbers can be checked against it.

## Definitions

| Outcome | Counts as | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Acted (replied "done", or did the thing) | positive | explicit reply |
| Tapped the notification | positive | tap-tracking redirect |
| Dismissed / not relevant | negative | explicit reply |
| No tap within 24 hours | negative (*inferred*) | hourly job |
| Snoozed | neutral, excluded from the rate | explicit reply |
| No response recorded | excluded from the rate | — |

When one notification has several signals, an explicit reply beats a tap, and a tap beats an inferred dismissal. Explicit and inferred results are reported separately, because they measure different things.

## Known biases in today's number

1. **Inferred dismissals are probably overstated.** The tap tracker only worked on the home network. A tap from a phone on cellular data was never recorded and would have been logged as a dismissal after 24 hours. All 3 negatives are of this kind.
2. **20 of 23 sends have no feedback at all.** They went out between 28 June and 6 July, before tap tracking existed. Excluding them is correct, but it leaves the sample tiny.
3. **One send may never have arrived.** The 4 August "Root rot call made, pot never opened" notification has an ID in the decision log but no delivery event.
4. **Silence isn't free either.** 6 of 8 silent decisions were failures (the language model call failed or cited evidence that didn't exist), not judgments. A good dismiss rate built on an engine that often fails to run would be misleading, so failures are reported next to the rate.
5. **One user, who built it.** The builder knows what the system is trying to do and may respond more charitably (or harshly) than a stranger.

## What makes it meaningful

- **Explicit replies.** Messages arriving by text, where you can answer *done*, *snooze* or *not relevant*, replace guesswork with labels. The rate will be reported on explicit labels first.
- **At least 20 rated interruptions** before judging against the target, then a rolling 30-day window.
- **Delivery confirmed per message**, so lost messages aren't counted as ignored.
- **More than one user** before any claim beyond "it works for its builder."

## Reproduce

```
python3 eval/dismiss_rate.py                       # all time
python3 eval/dismiss_rate.py --since 2026-08-01    # a window
python3 eval/dismiss_rate.py --json                # per-item detail
```

The script opens the database read-only.
